description:
The provided image displays three bar charts—labeled (a) WikiText, (b) an unlabeled dataset (likely a different benchmark), and (c) C4—each illustrating the relationship between perplexity and the number of quantization bits for two different methods: "Uniform" and "Ours." In each chart, the horizontal axis represents the "Quantization Bits," with values of 3, 4, 8, and 16. The vertical axis, labeled "Perplexity," measures the model's performance, with lower values indicating better performance. The bars are grouped by quantization bit level, with the "Uniform" method represented by dark blue bars and the "Ours" method by orange bars.

In chart (a) WikiText, the "Uniform" method shows a perplexity of approximately 29.2 for 3 bits, decreasing to about 26.6 for 4 bits, 26.5 for 8 bits, and 26.7 for 16 bits. The "Ours" method starts at a perplexity of about 21.8 for 3 bits, decreases to around 19.0 for 4 bits, 18.5 for 8 bits, and 18.5 for 16 bits. In chart (b), the "Uniform" method exhibits a perplexity of approximately 400 for 3 bits, decreasing to about 320 for 4 bits, 302 for 8 bits, and 304 for 16 bits. The "Ours" method shows a perplexity of about 255 for 3 bits, decreasing to around 175 for 4 bits, 180 for 8 bits, and 180 for 16 bits. In chart (c) C4, the "Uniform" method has a perplexity of approximately 29.2 for 3 bits, decreasing to about 25.3 for 4 bits, 24.9 for 8 bits, and 24.9 for 16 bits. The "Ours" method starts at a perplexity of about 20.8 for 3 bits, decreasing to around 18.4 for 4 bits, 18.0 for 8 bits, and 18.0 for 16 bits. Across all three datasets, the "Ours" method consistently achieves lower perplexity than the "Uniform" method at each quantization level, indicating superior performance.
